I have been playing fighting games for over 20 years, competing in national tournaments when I was younger. These days, I'm more of a casual player, preferring Smash Bros over typical fighting games since typical fighting games are harder to get into (you need to spend a lot of time learning moves, practicing, etc.). I'm also a huge fan of Dragon Ball. I've been reading Dragon Ball since Goku and I were both just kids. I grew up with Dragon Ball and it has affected my life in positive ways.

As a fan of Dragon Ball and fighting games, I love this game.

As a fighting game, the game is fun and very easy to start. Even if you're new to fighting games, the training mode is very helpful for starters. The game's auto combos are also great for new players. Once you get familiar with the game and want more advanced tactics, there's plenty here to keep you interested. There's really no reason any Dragon Ball fan new to fighting games should be afraid to give this a start.

As a Dragon Ball game, this game is a love letter to Dragon Ball fans. Hardcore Dragon Ball fans will immediately recognize that many of the basic moves used by characters are actually taken straight from the series. One of Krillin's kicks is a kick he used against Goku during a tournament (when they were kids). Freeza's elbow attack is the one he used against Goku. Likewise, the elbow attack Goku uses is the one he used against Freeza. The game is loaded with these. :D While the story mode isn't great, it has many references to the series and has many interesting interactions between characters in a "what if" situation (like Nappa being upset with Vegeta for obvious reason). Watching these scenes made me all giddy.

Overall, this is an excellent Dragon Ball game that no fan of Dragon Ball should miss.

Dragon Ball FighterZ, the revolutionary anime fighter that finally showed the world what a GOOD fighting game based on a popular show could really achieve. But is it still worth your time and money? Let's delve into it a bit.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
FighterZ, due to its rather large nature, has too many positives to list. Instead I will cover what I believe are the most beneficial positives as reasons to get the game.

[b][u]Fantastic Art Style[/u][/b]
The art style of FighterZ is something to behold. With absolutely beautiful cell shading, gigantic explosions and beams that do the show justice, the entire game almost looks like the manga / anime came alive onto your screen. The art, paired with the near flawlessly smooth animations, do the fights of the source material justice, unlike many previous titles that despite however good they may have been, were just "good for an anime game" at best. The fact they looked like marionettes dancing around didn't help.

[b][u]Picture-Perfect Replication of the Source Material[/u][/b]
This is a more subtle strength of the game, but I think it's worthy of mention. ArcSystem clearly watched the ENTIRE show and all the movies just to make this game. With very few exceptions, almost every single move in the game is a direct copy of a move in the show that character used. (Obviously not including characters that never actually fought seriously in the originals, such as Android 18) This even extends to basic moves, such as Broly's down-heavy and ki blasts, Kid Buu's underground stomp mediums, etc etc. The incredibly and frankly insane level of replication is worthy of immense praise. The fact that nearly none of the normal moves or Supers were made up without using the source material is incredible.

[b][u]Easy to Learn, Hard to Master[/u][/b]
Unlike a lot of fighting games, in which every individual character has their own specific circle turns required, button inputs, yadda yadda, FighterZ uses a very basic system. Every Super and basic premade combos are universal inputs, and many special attacks share inputs as well. This system encourages players to experiment with as many characters as they want, instead of being the one dude who looked at all the full-circle inputs for Hugo on Street Fighter, looked down at his Xbox controller D-Pad, and immediately gave up. However, the mechanics in FighterZ are also much deeper than they appear. The combo potential for every character, including jump canceling, reflecting at the right time, proper reflect baiting, etc, gives so much room for improvement.

[b][u]References Everywhere[/u][/b]
The absolute BEST praiseworthy aspect of FighterZ is the love letter it has written to long time fans of the material. FighterZ is absolutely OVERFLOWING with references, heartwarming interactions between old friends, and if you take the time to really crack open Story Mode, humorous and fascinating opinions the characters have on certain outlooks. Nearly every single time a character opens their mouth, it takes you right back to the show / manga you originally fell in love with.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
While FighterZ may be a fantastic anime game, it has no shortage of glaring problems as well for prospective players. The ones Ive listed below are the most problematic of the bunch and are things I believe prospective buyers should be aware of before purchasing.

[b][u]Story Mode and Arcade are Kinda Sh*t[/u][/b]
The major problem with the game is the lack of any decent content outside of online play. Story Mode alternates between pathetically easy at lower levels, with AI basically never even moving, to absolute omnipotent gods at high levels that can punish a 6 frame jab with a Level 3 80% of the time. Arcade is much of the same, except enemies enjoy a hefty damage increase of around 40% max, meaning that even the most basic of combos will still cripple all your characters. Its the same trashy single-player fighting game design we've all come to know and hate.

[b][u]Skilled Opponents Won't Let You Play[/u][/b]
As I previously mentioned, FighterZ has a wealth of deep mechanics to master for dedicated fighting game players. However, for anyone looking for a casual option, this game is no better than any other fighting games. A skilled opponent will have an answer to EVERY single thing you throw at them, and will usually counter you with ease before performing their maximum damage perfectly optimized corner combo loop to keep you in unbreakable hitstun for over 30 seconds. And you can't even defend against them, because they also have an answer to all your blocking techniques and can perfectly crack you open so fast you don't even properly learn what went wrong. Like all fighting games, this is a huge, glaring problem that is NEVER fixed properly due to generally inaccurate matchmaking skill levels. It will take you hours to ever stand a chance in online play.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
FighterZ is, despite the pretty exterior, a fighting game through and through. Any previous fan of the Dragon Ball franchise will get great satisfaction at all the jokes and references intended for them, but will find their dedication severely tested if you attempt to get deeper into the game mechanics. Be prepared to spend hundreds upon hundreds of hours grinding away to even rival the players you meet online, let alone defeat them. Story Mode and Arcade are functional, but have their own clear flaws after a while of playing. 

I would recommend this only for people who are great fans of the franchise and can tolerate the mediocre story combat for the character interactions, or people looking for a very good fighting game they don't mind sinking months into. If you don't fit either of those descriptions, FighterZ may be a risky purchase for you.

I enjoy the game, but I can't recommend it as a product in its current state for two reasons:
1. Though this is not mentioned on the store page and can only be found at the very bottom of their EULA, DBFZ does include Denuvo DRM, stripping legal customers of true ownership of the game. If this had been clearly labelled on the store page like it is with most Denuvo games, I wouldn't have bought the game.
2. DBFZ uses Easy Anti Cheat, which does support Steam Deck, but the developers chose not to click the box to enable Linux support, so the game will only work on Steam Deck and Linux if you disable EAC, preventing most online play. Online Play is a pretty significantly large reason to play the game, as it is a fighting game, so I figured I'd mention. I actually did know this going in, and chose to deal with it since I have a friend who is willing to disable EAC on their end to play with me (+ the game was like 85% off), but for your average Linux user, definitely avoid this game until it gets fixed. Pros
- Amazingly in depth combo system.
- Easy to pick up but incredibly difficult to master.
- Jaw dropping special moves.
- All characters are relatively balanced, with some being obviously stronger but none are unplayable necessarily.
- Destructive/Dramatic finishes still make me giddy 200+ hours later.
- My computer is essentially run by a hamster on a wheel and I can run it on the highest graphics.
- You can see how good or bad the connection is before you play someone online.
- The tag team system is incredible and extends combos far beyond their natural limitations.

Cons
- The story mode, except for my waifu Android 21, is subpar at best
- Steep learning curve (Not necessarily a con but you will get your shit pushed in for a while online and especially in competitive).
- No punishment for leavers in online matches, and you won't get the win if they do leave. (However when people leave too many times their name shows up as purple in lobbies and you can choose to decline them).
- As someone relatively high up on the competitive ladder (500,000+ BP) I can state without a doubt that this is the most corner oriented fighting game I've ever seen, some characters like Cell and Hit can pull off otherwordly combos when they have their opponent pinned to the side of the screen.
- The game with the season pass is honestly pretty pricey, but I love this game to death so I personally didn't mind.

Meh
- Arcade mode is rather reptitive, just like the story mode, but you can unlock Goku Blue and Vegeta Blue instead of buying them as DLC if you do well enough, plus the mode earns you a ton of in game currency you can use to get alternate costumes and such.
- A lot of the time your performance in game is dependent on how patient you are, if you try to mash buttons while you're being combo'd you're going to immediatlely be swept up in another combo that takes half, if not more of your health. But when you land those ridiculous combos one after another and make an amazing 1 v 3 comeback you won't be complaining.

Overall
I'd give this game a 9/10, because I can't stress enough how unique and addicting this game is. It has a few flaws both in the gameplay and in its matchmaking/lobby system, but in my opinion the mechanics, graphics, and artstyle more than make up for it. Honestly a near perfect rendition of a 2D fighting Dragon Ball game.

Ok, let's tackle this game shall we? This game, is freaking good, and I mean it when I say it's good. You can see there is a lot of passion put into this game, and true knowledge of the Dragon Ball universe, full voice acting of various languages, a story mode, arcade mode, overworld that you can do alot of stuff, online gameplay, combo challenges, great gameplay with outstanding graphics and so it goes, BUT it has it's weaknesses. 

First things first story mode, I'm glad it's here, and it took me around 15 hours to beat, BUT, you'll be fighting a bunch of potatoes, there is not a single challenging fight in the whole story mode, and it gets repetitive really fast, so those 15 hours might hurt. The amazing thing about the story are the character interactions, setting up different parties to see how they talk to each other in some very funny to watch cutscenes  with full voice acting to each character. The story itself is just an excuse to gather the cast and make they punch things, it's meh, but it works. You'll unlock Android 21 after you finish all the segments in the story mode.

Arcade mode, present in 3 different "courses" that have a normal and hard mode, you can unlock Goku and Vegeta SSGSS in the arcade, if you beat two courses being able to score at least an A rank at the end, it's fun single player memes to enjoy, and i'm glad there is a way to unlock the characters without the purchase.

The overworld, this is a pretty cute feature, you'll walk around and talk to NPCs that can take you to each activity in the game, there are also other players that you can interact with and create rooms to fight with a bunch of people, and that removes the wait of the matchmaker. You earn Zeni in the game, and gaining 300k and 500k zeni will also unlock you vegeta SSGSS and Goku SSGSS respectively, again, very nice. Zeni can be used to purchase capsules that contain avatar skins, colour for characters, announcers for the fights, a bunch of cool stuff to unlock. 

To the online now, it's important to note that I'm playing in the South America server, so I'm not the best example of game population, but the matchmaker can take some time to find matches. It's nice that you can select the desired connection you want to play with and skill level so the match will be smooth and balanced. Now how does ranked work? You'll fight other players in a best of 3 match, and after the match ends you'll get points,  as you gain more points, you'll rise in rank, if you lose points, you lose rank.

And last but not least, the combat, the gameplay, so how is it? It's nice, yet chaotic, and very unforgiving, if you are a fighting game fan you'll most likely enjoy the game, and it's Marvel vs Capcom esque style, with teams of 3 that can tag in and out and call for support attacks. The auto combo system allows for a new player to get into the game faster, but a good player will stray from this and learn a bunch of combos and synergy between characters, and here might be the pickle of the situation. Like I said, chaotic, and unforgiving, it feels great to deliver a massive combo and chain supers from all your team, the problem in my eyes is that you can sometimes delete an enemy character with a good combo, or nearly kill it, if your enemy mess up, you'll juggle him like a sack of potatoes left to right for several seconds without much the enemy can do to escape this punishment, and the same works for you, i've seen combos that simply delete one of my team members before I can even say shit. So if this hypes you to get online and destroy people getting the cinematic endings, those are really cool btw, this game is for you. But if you just want to play this because you're a dragon ball fan and you don't really have interest in going online, I would probably wait for a price drop, when the full deluxe xxx edition comes out with all characters from DLC and stuff, because this game doesn't have enough single player content to sustain it's full price, xenoverse 2 has the better single player dragon ball fun, but not the more serious combat system that FighterZ has, if you're paying the whole thing for this game, you should play the online.

So for the TL;DR
If you're a fan of fighting games, go right for it, it's a great and fun game.
If you're just a dragon ball fan wanting to play around for a bit, I would wait for a price drop. But if you're too hungry for the action, this a great game.

This game isn't just a fighting game to me, this game is something else, something special if you will. I was a Dragon Ball fan for as long as i can remember, watching the original series up until the end of Super. Throughout the years i have been waiting for THAT Dragon Ball game, the one that would transcend fans of the series and can just enjoy alone and with a buddy or two. Dragon Ball FighterZ scratched that itch. From the first trailer i could see that this game was gonna be a HUGE thing. I pre-ordered it for $80 and i can tell you now, as college student who's daily meal consists of noodle packs that cost less than a dollar, that this game is worth every single penny i threw at it. 

Story:
This is probably the weakest aspect of the game because it is so inconsistent. The writing is awesome with a lot of cool character interactions and nailing their mannerisms and ideals. the addition of Android 21 as a antagonist is also fresh in the sense that there we get to see a new Dragon Ball baddy as supposed to recycling villains already established in the lore. For a new charcater she fits in well with the rest of the cast and is a good standalone character. However the main weakness of the story is how the story is structured. You have to fight through wave after wave of weak ass clones to get to the "boss" of the stage and move on, all while saving other familiar Dragon Ball characters. The problem with this is that it makes battles extremely boring since there is no proper build up to those fights. Something like a netherrealm style big story mode would have been a lot better. 

Visuals and Sound:
This. Game. Looks. AWESOME. The game's presentation is excellent. Characters look detailed and move fluidly across the screen. Particle effects are large and in your face but not distracting enough to take you out of the action. The dynamic camera everytime you use a super is excellent, it brings you closer to the action and gives a awesome visual flare that makes the game that much more fun to play. The close up of Piccolo's face and seeing his veins when he uses Light Grenade, seeing the Cell's smug smile when using Solar Kamehameha, the spinning camera when Gohan uses the Father-Son Kamehameha stopping behind him to reveil Goku standing behind him, its all done beautifully. The game's dramatic starts and finishes provide fanservice and visual flare that makes the game all the better. I only wished there were more "what if" dramatic finishes but with the amount there are already i can't complain. The soundtrack and voices in this game are also stellar. With both the option of Japanese and English voices and each character having their own theme. Although some voice actors are underplayed or overplayed depending the overall performances of the cast are really good. Especially the Japanese voice actor for Broly and the english voice actor for Vegeta.

Gameplay:
This game made me love fighting games. This game is the pinacle of easy to play but hard to master. It uses a system inspired by Marvel vs Capcom 3 and added to it. This game does have two autocombo buttons but to do optimal damage you need to know a lot of tricks of the trade and explore the mechanics within the game or if you want to play with auto combos you can as well.It feels really god to learn something in this game as you see it pull off on screen you feel a sense of pride and joy. While i will say i'm not the best at this game (i'm average at best) it is still a blast to play. Never before has losing looked and felt so good. 

In summary:
Graphics, visuals and Presentation: 10/10
Gameplay: 9/10
Story: 7.3/10
Sound: 9.8/10
Fun factor: 10/10
Overall: 9.8/10
BUY. IT. NOW

The game takes place sometime between "Universe 6" and "Future Trunks" arcs of Dragon Ball Super. The game's main antagonist, Android 21 (or later, her evil-half), was a normal human who eventually became an Android created by the Red Ribbon Army after her son became the model for Android 16. Once she awakens, she repairs 16 and uses the Dragon Balls to resurrect Frieza, Cell, Nappa, and the Ginyu Force, and seals away the powers and souls of all of Earth's strongest warriors. Wanting to control the hungry monster within her, she and 16 develop a linking system originally created by Dr. Gero in which a human soul (the player) can possess the warriors and provide them strength.

      ●There are 3 Arc's in Dragon Ball FighterZ
 
           ● Super Warrior Arc

      This is the first Arc of the game, and in it we play the role of the “player's soul.” After “possessing” Goku, we wake up to Bulma, according to whom Goku has amnesia. After a short further explanation of what is happening, you go in search of your comrades to create a strong team with which to defeat the main villain in this Arc - Android 21.

          ● Enemy Warrior Arc

   In the second Arc you are given the opportunity to "possess" the body of an main villain from the anime. You play with it, form a team of villains, and then even make a joint team between villains and heroes to beat Android 21.

Now, let's begin the review.


[h1]Dragon Ball FighterZ is...[/h1]


[h1]+ very Dragon Ball.[/h1]

A fighting game's got to have sick characters, and a Dragon Ball game's got to have sick Dragon Ball characters.

Thankfully, this game's got a bunch of sick Dragon Ball characters. DBFZ features series staples like Goku, Vegeta, and Freiza, and even features some unexpected, but welcome, characters like Nappa, Captain Ginyu, and Tien. Dragon Ball fans should have no problem finding at least a few characters they like in this game.

What's really great about this game's cast is how well its characters have been faithfully adapted to the game from the source material. From signature moves to basic punches and kicks to character mannerisms, nearly everything in this game is a reference to the Dragon Ball source material.

When you couple faithful character adaptations with Arc System Work's anime graphics magic, you get this game, the most Dragon Ball game in existence so far.


[h1]+ a satisfying gameplay experience.[/h1]

Expect speed, movement, oppressive offense, and long combos. This is a fighting game in the same vein as the Marvel vs. Capcom series, so DBFZ is definitely one of the faster-paced fighting games around. A lot of what I say in this section applies to a lot of fighting games, but my words apply to DBFZ especially.

There's a lot of fun to be had with DBFZ if you're interested in high-speed action.

Connecting with an attack in the open, mounting pressure, breaking defense, and doing big combos are all immensely satisfying. The game's much more stressful when you're on the defensive, but punishing an opponent for being risky or predictable during his/her offense can be just as satisfying and any offensive moment you make.

Basically, the game's a blast as long as you play well (by your own standards). When you make even just a few great gameplay moments happen, the game's fun regardless of whether you win or lose.

Furthermore, like any competitive game, this game only gets better as you get better. I mean, of course you would have more fun the more often you do sick stuff in the game.

Also note that, in this section, I've praised the game without ever mentioning the Dragon Ball franchise. I would play DBFZ even if it weren't a Dragon Ball game. DBFZ's just a blast. This game has the deep and satisfying gameplay I crave as a fighting game fan.


[h1]+ accessible and uncompromised.[/h1]

DBFZ is probably one of the easiest fighting games to learn and play around. In DBFZ, characters have few moves, combos have a straight-forward structure, and move execution doesn't get more complex than a half-circular motion on the stick/dpad/whatever.

You do have to learn how to play three characters, though.

If you've never played fighting games competitively, DBFZ is a great game to start with.

If you've played fighting games before, particularly 2D airdash-y fighting games like BlazBlue, Guilty Gear, Melty Blood, or Marvel vs. Capcom, you're going to take to this game very, very quickly.

Now, after I've just told you how easy this game is, let me tell you how hard this game is. This game's easy to play, but not easy to play well. It's a classic case of easy to learn, hard to master.

I remember reading an excellent quote on the internet somewhere. Please forgive me for forgetting your name, random internet user. The quote goes something like this: "DBFZ is easy to play, but when you play someone better than you, you don't get to play."

Truer words have never been written.


[h1]+ very playable online.[/h1]

DBFZ uses a delay-based netcode, meaning online matches have slightly more input lag than offline matches. It's a bit of a shame that delay is always going to be a factor, but the truth of the matter is that DBFZ feels fine online.

Most of the matches I've played have felt very good. Rarely have I played any matches I'd classify as laggy.

The following is kind of a side note, but I suppose it's relevant to the topic of lag:

I'd say that most of my online matches on PC feel less laggy than offline matches I've played on PS4. The PS4 version unfortunately features a noticable amount of input lag, while the PC version doesn't.

I haven't played any online matches on the PS4 version. Maybe if I had, I would have a completely different opinion about how DBFZ plays online. My guess is that I probably wouldn't like the experience.


[h1]- somewhat unreliable online.[/h1]

DBFZ's lobbies have connection issues, and the game's "ring match" sub lobbies are buggy. Expect to be randomly booted from lobbies and to be unable to rejoin a ring match that you were previously able to join.

DBFZ's lobbies are surprisingly flawed given how Arc System Works has made better functioning lobby systems before for their more recent Guilty Gear and BlazBlue games. I've never had problems with lobbies in those games before.

I wouldn't call DBFZ's unreliable lobby systems deal breakers, but I would call them painful to deal with.


[h1]- somewhat imbalanced.[/h1]

Character balance is a bit of an issue in DBFZ. The balance isn't so bad that some characters are broken and some characters are too weak to be playable, but there's definitely a sizeable power difference between the best characters and the rest of the characters.

Right now, Adult Gohan, Android 16, and Cell are the kings of the game. All three of these characters are the best at something and are good at about everything.

I've gotta stop myself here though. You're here for a review, not my "expert"-level [strike]complaints[/strike] character analyses.

I suppose it's cool that these characters are sick, but it's not really cool that everyone else is notably less sick.


[h1]? a repetitive but amusing story.[/h1]

DBFZ includes a story mode campaign. The story's predictable, and the fights against CPUs can get repetitive, but the character interactions are highly amusing.

The story mode is only barely worth playing for unlocking Android 21 and seeing Dragon Ball characters interact with one another.


[h1]? a bit of a chore depending on who you are.[/h1]

I don't like unlocking characters for fighting games. In fact, I'm not interested in unlocking things in general. I'm more interested in the grind of getting better at a game than I am in the grind of unlocking game content.

I know there are people out there that find satisfaction in unlocking things in games, so I don't want to mark DBFZ down for having three characters be unlockables.

Whether you like unlocking content or not, I think it's best that you are aware that Android 21, SSGSS Goku, and SSGSS Vegeta are locked from the start of the game.


[h1]... an excellent Dragon Ball game and an excellent fighting game.[/h1]

If you're interested in fighting games, this is the game for you to try. DBFZ's a nice and easy introduction to fighting games, and is a quality fighting game itself. You might want to wait for a sale, but personally, I would have bought this game even at full price, even if it weren't a Dragon Ball game. I just really like how DBFZ plays.

If you like Dragon Ball and aren't really interested in fighting games, I still think this game is worth a try. Depending on how big a fan you are of Dragon Ball, you might want to wait for this game to go on sale. There's a lot of Dragon Ball goodness here to admire.

If you like Dragon Ball and you like fighting games, then DBFZ is an easy recommendation, even at full price. You probably already have the game. I have no idea why you're reading this review. Thanks for reading, though!

I love this game. It is a visual treat and perhaps the greatest Dragon Ball game to date. However, it has one of the most frustrating online experiences ever. The game is in perhaps one of its worst states of balance since release; Fusions, Labcoat 21, and Broly have ruled the meta for more than a year. Worse than the fact that the meta is stale, is the fact that the meta is entirely DLC characters, making this game decidedly PTW in that aspect. I recommend getting the DLC characters anyway, because they are great fun, but the power-creep of the game is self-evident.

Casual play is sweatier than ranked, and you will routinely encounter individuals triple or quadruple your rank.

Mechanically, this game is great, but unless you watch online tutorials and lab for hours upon hours, you will quickly reach a point where the mechanical skill of your opponents dramatically outclasses your own. Even before you reach that point, smurfs abound in the lowers echelons of ranked, either intentional ones who ruin the fun of others, or players who have switched platforms and won't give you a second glance as they climb back to their old rank. Wi-Fi players are everywhere, and until rollback is implemented at an undisclosed future date, matchmaking connectivity is often miserable, even with ethernet.

The Campaign is laughably mediocre at best, and is by no means the main draw of the game, and while some of the what-if scenarios are fun, it largely boils down to mashing the "skip dialogue" button until you get to the next fight.

This game is great to play with friends casually, and has a strong competitive scene, but if you want to take this game seriously, be prepared for a slog of laggy games, smurfs, a ridiculously high learning curve for mechanics, and rage quits that the game doesn't punish.

I’m not usually a fighting-game person, but liking shorter games this has ended up as the game I have clocked the most hours into. And for the most part, I’ve enjoyed it. It’s fun and challenging and is a good contrast to other games I like to chill out and play. Even though I’m a noob in fighting games, I wouldn’t call this necessarily beginner friendly. It does try really hard in some areas, it has auto-combos for beginners, and if I had to set a difficulty to it, I suppose it’s easy to learn/hard to master. ArcSys knows that a lot of people probably will try it out because it’s Dragon Ball, so they do try their best.

FighterZ has ran smoothly on my computer for about a year now. Since it’s been a while for me personally to have major issues, I’ll still recommend this game to anyone who knows their computer can run it.

Tutorials: Season 3 has added a lot here, with the FighterZ Dojo and the Tournament of Power competition. It was bare bones before, and no real help for anything besides beginner knowledge. And I would call it useless doing it separately outside the Story Mode, which you’re stuck doing the basics for a while into it. Now, I’ll say all the tutorials together are something substantial and having a character set to be your master is an interesting concept and incentive for someone to complete them. Not my cup of tea, but it’s cool for people who like it.

Training Mode in general: There’s enough variety in what you can look at plus controlling the settings where you can spend hours effectively trying to get better. If you know what you’re doing, this game gives you a lot here to find strategies and teams that work for you. The combo challenges are nice if only so you can get a feel to see what sort of moves go together well for what character.

Story: The story itself is fine, but the pacing for both the story and gameplay is awful. It’s nice that it has that gallery option if you just want to revisit fun interactions and dialogue between the characters. That’s the best part of story mode. Like I said for tutorials, until you unlock hard mode a huge chunk of story is just repeating tutorials and super easy fights. I would only recommend story for Android 21 unlock and zeni grinding, though the ToP challenges in the Dojo eclipse the latter now.

Arcade Mode: I was tired of the same sets of fights, so I almost gave this mode up until it introduced random. Now, I go through it if I want to practice a few matches with a team without deciding what CPU level and teams to fight against. Just fight what the game gives me and roll with it. Not too hard, and I don’t know what the difficulty curve is set to, but it works if I don’t feel like going online. 

Local Battle: I don’t have any friends who play this game, so I can’t comment on its usefulness there. Looks competent. If I do have a specific CPU level I want to try, or just a single character to practice without doing a whole 3v3 battle I use this mode for quick fights.

Online: I only do normal matches, so I can’t comment on the Party Matches or anything that isn’t simply being matched with someone for battle. I don’t know anyone else that plays the game, and I feel party and ring matches are best used among people you know and know your fighting style. I see people unhappy with what matches are offered to them, but for me the longer I’ve had this game the better it is.

New chances: I can set my parameters to good internet connection, high completion rate, and someone around my skill level and have matches lined up. It’s not always great, but I’ll accept a few poor nights of not much compared to my old luck. Old chances: Have to accept all kinds of challengers, with poor internet connection, possible rage-quitters and people way out of my skill level and sometimes still have nothing. Part of it may be that I’m not completely at the bottom of the barrel with skill level now and more people exist that are better at the game and matched with me, yet overall, it’s a huge difference to the first 6 months or so I had at the game.

I won’t discount people who say they have a horrible time finding a match, everyone’s connection story and luck will be different, but for me I haven’t had head-banging problems in a while.

DLC: I paid for all the passes (not including Ultimate), though the first season pass was on sale when I bought it with the game. Disclosure done, I think they’re all okay. I always have at least one DLC character on my team, if not two. I can’t say on what average tier they fall into, not knowledgeable enough on all of them or fighting games, but I can say that none really feel same-y to me, and that’s what I care about when putting extra money on something. Some have similar moves – which is likely to happen with several variety of Saiyans including Goku, Vegeta, Broly and fusions – yet they’re all mixed up in ways where none feel like they have the same exact play style.

Unless you feel it’s worth the investment, I’ll look up videos on characters you’re interested in buying or just go for characters you like, no harm in that. I wouldn’t buy the newest season 3 pass with only [i]hopes[/i] that your favorite character will make it in. Wait until they are confirmed at least if that’s the only character you’re interested in.

I wanted a new, decent fighter with a heavy focus on combos and multiple characters per fight à la Skullgirls/mvc/kof starring draginbollz characters and guess what, my wish got granted. Thanks Shenron!

[b]But is it good? You bet it is![/b]

+ Gorgeous visuals with the state-of-the-art team red rendering pipeline for characters (look at their GDC guilty gear conference for more detail, crazy use of UV mapping!) which looks INSANELY GOOD on dragon ball characters!
Crazy simple technically yet crazy beautiful effects with generous feedback for every attack and supers all over the place! (7 meter levels and you can DHC (cancel supers into other character supers) allowing for super flashy displays and finishers!

+ Decent content with a cool story mode and a good amount of base playable characters.

+ Super fast-paced gameplay with easy to perform combos (in general, not just autocombos which are pretty bad given they pop out a dragon ball, have meh/ok-ish damage and end up in a soft knockdown).

+ Some characters have really great gameplay. Nappa is a juggernaut/hulk that uses saibaimen with their own AI (cf: Jack-O from GG) for pressure, Beerus can ricochet his projectiles with every attack, Tien/c16 have crazy one-time lv3's, and ginyu can use his signature move! Yes He can swap with the opposing character (and also heavily gimp him because he can't use his squad moves!), making him viable despite his weakness! Also Yamcha is super, SUPER strong!


[b]It does have its downsides, though[/b]:

- Expensive ! Base pricing at launch is 60 bucks + 35 for the season pass making it reach almost 100€$ if you want to have all characters! Arcsys as a whole seems to become greedy lately, with blazblue crosstag battle having half of it's cast being DLC and 4 season passes, this is bad!

- The game "menu" is basically guilty gear xrd rev2's online lobby mode: You move around as a chibi in an ONLINE hub world. Although this one is well made, quirky and ergonomic enough, serverside lags could ruin your experience. I might not have encountered annoying latency yet but I have heard people complain about it a lot so be careful about this.

Imagine this: It is 2018 and Dragon Ball Z fighting games were always very simple. 2 attack buttons, Ki button, and no command inputs. It was like that for a long time. That all changed when Arc System, mainly the Guilty Gear devs, came in and made this game. It completely changes Dragon Ball Z fighting games and makes it play like the older games, but let's not get ahead of ourselves, we will get there very soon. We just want to see if Bandai publishing this game was a good idea (it was).

Story: This game has a story, and I will use the story from the mode. In the 3 playable arcs, the main story is about a new Android named Android 21, who is a female android with the appearance of a Majin race. The 3 arcs are about the Z Fighters and new allies teaming up to fight this threat. Plus, clones are appearing and wreaking havok and energy waves are weakening the fighters, so links have to be made to regain strength. The script was written by Akira Toriyama himself, so there is some depth to it, but there are flaws, like how the arcs are not arcs, just different perspectives, and how gameplay and story is imbalanced, with lots of plot that can probably be simplified, but hey, it's not all bad, as there are plenty of character interactions that you can get and some pretty funny moments, but I still feel it could be improved, because honestly, the story mode sucks. Besides the interactions, all you do is mop the floor with the same clones that don't play differently from the regular characters. Yeah, there are skills, but most players will just overpower the skills the opponents use and end up getting skills that are much stronger, and there are some poorly written scenes, mainly the Android Arc with seemingly forced deaths. However, I won't spoil, but trust me, you can see the forced deaths when they happen, but feel free to DM me if you are confused about the deaths I am talking about.

Gameplay: Here we go. Forgoing the simple gameplay of previous fighting games, this game takes a lot form Guilty Gear: 3 attack buttons and a unique attack called "Special" (for simplicity I will call it the Ki button) and you can use command inputs like QCF for special moves, which is becoming worringly rare these days. The main fighting is set up in a 3v3 style, with the ability to call assists, both characters as well, making for some hectic games. Learning combos is very fun and simple, yet, challenging for the more dynamic combos, and while beginners can still have fun with the simple combos and auto-combo, more experienced players can make longer combos and take advantage of the auto-combo system which can get crazy. Have a character or 2 down? Use your Sparking, which buffs you in many ways as a sort of comeback mechanic, or you can get the Dragon Balls by doing combos or auto-combos, summon Shenron, and make a wish. That is crazy, and the hectic gameplay makes it fun!

Online: The main focus of this game is the online with all the modes. You have the standard ranked and casual, as well as ring matches to help play with friends, and Arena, which is just another Casual match. What is new is a party mode which allows up to 6 players at once in a fight in the 3v3 format. Teamwork is key.... or just carry the entire team, whatever works. There are also special boss events where 3 players can fight a boss character for rewards, and they can get pretty fun. Unfortunately, the netcode is terrible. Despite rollback being what all fighting games should go for, ArcSys stayed in the past and used delay based netcode, causing 7 frame delays to be a standard playing the game. Also, no crossplay either. 3 seasons in and ArcSys showed no interest in changing this. However, one thing that heavily damages online is the rage quitters. especially on PC. For some reason, Arc System just won't punish rage quitters, causing them to multiply! They even rage quit when you are not in ranked. Ouch. The only thing to not run into a rage quitter is through settings or checking their square, and the game tells you complete jack about the squares. Honestly they need to punish rage quitters, every other game does that. Smash Ultimate, Street Fighter V Arcade Edition, Marvel Vs. Capcom Infinite, and so much more. Get on it, Arc System!

Graphics and Presentation: Wow this game! This game uses a similar technique found in Guilty Gear, mainly the newer ones with animations and bone structures that emulate the animations of an anime, and they look great! They look so smooth and the cel-shading also looks great! There is even some battle damage implemented, but not too crazy. Just some scars, and armor cracks, but still a neat detail. I think more fighting games should have a battle damage feature. However, the backgrounds do not have this same style and look a little out of place, but they are destructible, so that makes up for it. You can also tell that Arc System were huge Dragon Ball fans through the character interactions through win quotes and even quotes mid match. They even include finishers called "Dramatic Finishes" activated by pressing Heavy (or Vanish if you use Freezer) which references moments in the show and a few what-is moments. And yes, you can Yamcha Yamcha.

Sound and Soundtrack: It's a broken record with Dragon Ball Z games and I won't have it any other way: Just use the sounds from the show. They sound great and fit well. You can't beat these sounds. Meanwhile, the OST is also pretty good in certain parts. It feels overpowered by the sound effects though, but what I heard is still good and catchy, even if Hit's theme is so unfitting.

Replayability: It's an online based game. 'Nuff said.

Final Thoughts: This game is great. Great gameplay, mostly great online, great graphics, awesome sounds, good music, it has it all. But what rating would I give it? My opinion, blah, I think this game gets an 8/10 with a side of Super Saiyan 4- oh that was retconned and people hated GT.... Well, the game is still good and I heavily recommend it. If you are more of a console gamer, the game is on PS4 (my OG place for playing the game), XBOX ONE, and Nintendo Switch (which came out later). If you are wondering about the Switch port, it is fantastic, it runs great, and features a unique resolution mechanic to help the Switch handle the game. Thanks open beta! Also, I am still waiting for them to add Master Roshi, I mean, come on, he trained Goku since the original Dragon Ball!

2020 Update: In Season 3, there were some substantial gameplay updates, like different Z Assists, changes to the meter and gameplay mechanics, alongside other neat changes

It's the ultimate fighting game for Dragonball fans where they can match up all their favourite characters in a fantasy matchup of Normal Goku vs Black Hair Goku vs Pink Hair Goku vs Young Goku vs White Hair Goku vs Cyan Hair Goku.

But seriously, this is where the essence of 3v3 tag battle spectacle went after Marvel vs Capcom is no longer something to marvel at for the forseeable future.

FighterZ is an offence oriented game with straightforward autocombos possible by repeatedly pressing a single attack button and a homing dash command that can get you quickly to your opponent no matter where they are on screen. More nuanced attack options are available to players who invest further time and knowledge into the game.

Defensive options come in the form of:
Down + Heavy universal anti-air/launcher
A punishable universal Back + Special parry command
Guard cancels where you can swap in an assist character at the cost of 1 bar
Random unsafe specials/supers

The training mode is very comprehensive and goes through movement options, attacks, defence options in a progressive manner. 
The training all goes to hell when you actually play versus battles, but this is a general syndrome in the fighter genre since the days of Street Fighter.

[i]As a rule of thumb when it comes to learning fighting games, focus on accomplishing little goals one at a time (how to block attacks, how to anti air, how to recognise when it is safe to come out of block and start pressing your own attacks) before thinking about winning matches.
Randomly pressing buttons without thought in a fighting game would be the equivalent of:
-swerving left and right randomly in a straight line in a racing game
-choosing random options in an rpg to attack, defend and use magic without paying attention to the battle
-not paying attention to boss patterns and just wildly attacking in action games such as Monster Hunter, Dark Souls, Bayonetta[/i]

For the solo player out there, it has a single player storyline campaign with light RPG/levelling elements and a standard arcade mode gauntlet with branching paths depending on your ingame performance. 

Controls are gamepad friendly, so a fightstick is not compulsory.
Specials do not have the dreaded dragon punch/Z motion (forward, down, downforward punch).
Supers are done through quartercircle motions and two buttons. No double quartercicle motions here.

One of the best looking 2d fighters to date though. If you want to just run through the singleplayer content, it's not a bad game to pick up especially on sale.

For many years, Dragon Ball Fans have consistently requested for a true actual Dragon Ball fighting game. Finally after the struggle we have one. Is it worth your time and money? We'll see.

[b] Story [/b]
With the new addition of Andriod 21 designed by Akira Toriyama, of course we are also introduced to a new story to accompany her. The story is divided up into 3 parts. Super Warrior Arc, Enemy Warrior Arc, and finally the Andriod 21 arc.
Each of the arcs sort of has it's own "perspective" What I mean by that is, in the Super Warrior Arc we can see Frieza and Cell get eaten and absorbed by Andriod 21 for her to grow stronger to fight her off in the final battle. However, in the Enemy Warrior Arc, Frieza and Cell are actually not eaten but rather help Goku in the final battle against Andriod 21. The actual "canon" story relating to Andriod 21, would have to be her own arc. If I'm to be completely honest with you. I didn't give two shits about the story. While I find it great with the cutscenes and voice acting which is absolutely amazing. The actual story... is actually pretty forgettable. 

[b] Gameplay [/b]
I will say this now. I believe Dragon Ball FighterZ to be THE BEST fighting game on the market currently. Dragon Ball FighterZ isn't a 1 on 1 fighting game. Rather, it's a 3 on 3 fighting game. The mechanics in Dragon Ball FighterZ are just amazing. This game just screams creativity. You can create some awesome, over the top creative flashy stuff, or some evil cheap crap to throw your opponents off. I love that! It allows the player to further dive into practice mode alot more often. Whenever I hop into practice mode, I always find out something new. I know of those who don't like the 3 on 3 combat style. However, believe me that it is absolutely amazing in this game. Now will all that's good comes with bad. The thing that sets the fire on the community and game are "auto combos" and it's understandable too. Essentially, auto combos are literally... AUTO COMBOS. You sit there, hit a button mutliple times until the combo ends. This promotes SPAMMING, this is in no way a good thing for players. Especially ones that are new and learning to play. Since the most common thing with newcomers to fighting games is spamming, here spamming actually looks like they are doing something. The auto combos have tracking, no matter how fluid your movement and cross up game is you will eventually get hit. This is absolutely disgusting. The thing with auto combos, they give you sort of "unique" types of strings or animations. For example, Trunks. Trunks has an auto combo string that leads into a crossup followup. It's really good but it's locked behind an auto combo. Therefore even influencing button mashing and spamming in the game. I believe this to be the absolute worse thing in this game.

[b] Graphics [/b]
The graphics in this game are absolutely amazing. After hearing that Arc Systems were making this I expected amazing visuals, and that is exactly what we got. You can increase resolution scaling to make the game look absolutely cripsy clear and clean. Arc Systems has probably the best looking anime games out there.

[b] Soundtrack [/b]
The soundtrack is this game is absolutely amazing. It captures that fighting spirit and motivation to improve your game. Every single track in this game is easy to remember and sounds great.

[b] Difficulty [/b]
Dragon Ball FighterZ isn't a hard game to pick up. It's really beginner friendly and encourages those who aren't exactly interested in fighting games to get into them. The tutorial is simple and clean, showing off tips and tricks you can do in this game. Arc Systems usually have great tutorials in their fighting games. My problem with this however, there are MULTIPLE things the game doesn't teach you, nor let you know of these. For example, did you know you can tag into another partner in your team without using your special and then switching to them? Did you know that if you dragon rush and hold a button down instead of 21 hits you get 31 for more damage? Did you know that if you press up, hold foward and press the right trigger you can do an easy Instant Air Dash compared to the manual way with the dpad or stick? The game doesn't tell you any of this. Now, this could be to encourage players to discover more in practice mode, but I personally believe that these are core mechanics of the game that should be shown to the player to make them aware.

[b] DLC Handling [/b]
I can't go exactly too much into detail since we don't the full roster of DLC characters, but I will try my best. I'm not going to refer to datamines or leaks, because I don't want to give false information. So far we know that there will be 8 new characters. So far we know 2 out of the 8. Bardock and Broly. the actual pricing of them is not confirmed yet however. I'll update this section of my review upon new information.

[b] Pricing [/b]
To be completely honest, I don't think Dragon Ball FighterZ is asking for TOO much... but the price could be reduced. 
The game's roster looks acceptable in my standards. But somtimes it just looks really damn small due to the 3 on 3 gameplay style. The roster includes fan favorite characters, I'm pretty sure everyone is completly fine with this base roster. 

[h1] Overall [/h1]
Dragon Ball FighterZ is an excellent game for newcomers and pros. As I said before, I believe this to be the best fighting game on the market currently. If you are looking for a fighting game, or you just like Dragon Ball, or you want to get into a fighting game that is easy on controls and mechanics then this is the game for you.

[h1] Overall Score: 9/10 [/h1]

DRAGON BALL FighterZ is a remarkably polished fighting game that captures the speed, spectacle, and personality of Dragon Ball while offering enough mechanical depth to function as a serious competitive fighter. Developed by Arc System Works and published by Bandai Namco Entertainment, it takes a traditional side-view fighting framework and transforms it into something that frequently resembles an interactive episode of the anime. The result is accessible enough to provide immediate entertainment while still demanding considerable practice from anyone hoping to master its deeper systems.

Combat is built around three-versus-three battles, with players selecting a trio of fighters before each match. Only one character fights directly at a time, but teammates can provide assists or be tagged into the battle. This structure creates an important strategic layer because a strong team is about more than selecting three individually powerful characters. Assists can extend combos, cover an approach, maintain offensive pressure, or create safer opportunities to switch characters. Managing the health of the entire team also matters, since withdrawing an injured fighter at the right moment can preserve them for a later comeback.

The controls strike an excellent balance between accessibility and complexity. Newcomers can quickly perform basic combinations, Super Dashes, Dragon Rush attacks, special techniques, and visually impressive super moves. It does not require extensive fighting-game knowledge simply to make something exciting happen on screen. Beneath that approachable surface, however, lies a much more demanding system involving movement, blocking, assists, meter usage, character positioning, combo optimization, pressure, counters, and team synergy. Skilled opponents expose just how much there is to learn, giving the game a substantial competitive ceiling.

Its visual presentation remains one of its greatest accomplishments. Although the characters are rendered as 3D models, clever animation and camera techniques make battles look remarkably similar to traditional Dragon Ball animation. Characters reproduce familiar poses, expressions, transformations, energy attacks, and signature techniques with tremendous attention to detail. Super moves temporarily turn fights into spectacular cinematic sequences filled with enormous blasts and dramatic camera angles. Environmental destruction and special dramatic moments further reinforce the feeling that these are genuine Dragon Ball confrontations rather than generic fighting matches wearing a licensed appearance.

The selection of fighters draws from across the franchise, bringing together famous heroes, villains, transformations, and supporting characters. Each character has recognizable abilities while fitting into the broader combat framework, making experimentation with different teams rewarding. Finding three fighters whose assists and strengths complement one another becomes an enjoyable part of learning the game. Additional characters released through FighterZ Passes significantly expand the available choices, although players wanting the broadest roster should keep in mind that much of that expanded selection comes from additional content.

For solo players, the game provides an original story featuring Android 21 alongside a large collection of familiar characters. Character interactions are entertaining, particularly for fans who enjoy seeing unusual combinations of heroes and villains communicate with one another. The campaign also provides a comfortable environment for becoming familiar with the mechanics. Its main weakness is repetition. Battles and progression can eventually feel routine, so the story is unlikely to remain as compelling as the multiplayer component once the novelty of its original scenario begins to fade.

Multiplayer is where the combat system has the greatest opportunity to shine. Human opponents introduce unpredictability that the single-player battles cannot consistently reproduce, forcing players to adapt their strategies rather than relying on familiar patterns. Competitive matches can become extremely intense, with rapid movement, long combinations, assists, substitutions, and powerful attacks occurring in quick succession. Local multiplayer also makes it a strong choice for playing directly against friends, particularly because the fundamental controls are approachable enough for less experienced participants to enjoy themselves.

That accessibility does not eliminate frustration for newcomers. Against experienced players, a mistake can lead to a lengthy combo and substantial damage before control is regained. Defensive knowledge becomes increasingly important as the competition improves, and the amount of visual activity can occasionally make hectic situations difficult to follow. Anyone expecting a simple Dragon Ball button-masher may therefore encounter a much steeper learning curve than anticipated. The game rewards patience and practice, especially once players move beyond casual battles.

Steam Deck compatibility requires some qualification. The game does not provide an ideal officially verified handheld experience, and online functionality can be affected by its anti-cheat implementation under SteamOS. Players may be able to run portions of the game through compatibility solutions, but it should not be treated as a straightforward, fully supported Steam Deck title, particularly if online multiplayer is the priority. For a game whose long-term appeal is strongly connected to competitive play, this limitation is important for Deck-focused buyers.

Despite its age and the expansion of its roster through paid content, the fundamental fighting experience remains exceptionally strong. Its greatest achievement is that the Dragon Ball license enhances an already capable fighting game rather than compensating for weak mechanics. Fans receive an impressive recreation of famous characters and attacks, while fighting-game enthusiasts receive a fast, technical, team-oriented system with considerable room for improvement and experimentation.

DRAGON BALL FighterZ succeeds as both a celebration of Dragon Ball and a substantial fighting game in its own right. The repetitive story structure, intimidating skill gap, additional character costs, and imperfect Steam Deck situation prevent it from being flawless, but its responsive combat, outstanding presentation, satisfying team mechanics, and enormous competitive depth make those shortcomings relatively easy to forgive. It remains an excellent choice for players who want Dragon Ball battles delivered with the structure and sophistication of a dedicated competitive fighter.

The last fighting game I played before this one was Tekken Tag Tournament for the PS2 so I been out of this genre for a long time.  I am, however, I fairly big fan of the dragon ball franchise.

Graphics are beautiful.  Every character looks amazing.  And even the backgrounds are very nice.  The art in this game is better than a lot of the art from the actual show.  The game uses a mini town hub to select what activity you want to participate in and everything looks competent there.  But all the gushing is really for the story mode cut scenes and the actual battles.  I really can't praise the graphics enough.

Music is pretty good.  It sounds "dragon ballish" if that makes any sense.  It's nothing you will find yourself wanting to jam outside of the game.  But it all seems to fit.

The sound is a mixed bag.  Mostly good.  One of the best things I want to point out is it seems to have the entire Japanese and English voice casts from the show.  I've watched the entire series in Japanese and English dubs.  If it ain't the cast from the show in each language then they need a freaking award for best imitations I've ever heard.  And you can switch between these freely in the sounds menu.  During combat it can get pretty noisy though.  It all sounds good - hits, combos and special attacks.  Characters have special voice lines when they do certain things.  But in certain situations it can all overlap a be a bit of overload.

Practice mode.  As someone who was away from the genre for a long time this mode was pretty important to me in the beginning.  I want to say overall it does a pretty good job at teaching you the basics of the game.  It does challenge you with some pretty dang difficult combo strings to pull off that seem unrealistic in actual matches with a live opponent.  But maybe I am just noob here and I will get to that later.

The game claims I am roughly half way through the story mode.  And I have to say it is fairly lengthy.  I don't know if that is par for the course nowadays for the genre.  But there are A LOT of cinematic scenes and dialogue.  An overall critique of the story itself is... eh.  It's there.  I won't spoil anything.  You can tell they put some effort in.  But even half way through I am still a bit confused about wtf is going on but maybe it will all make sense in the end.  There is also an item system that seems exclusive to this mode but for me it just makes the experience even more confusing.  I think they could have done without it.  Not a single encounter has been challenging.  I didn't see a difficulty option and maybe it has been ramping up at a snails pace.  They must have thought they had a top notch dragon ball esk story lined up that even if it's your first time playing a fighting game you could experience it.  The difficulty is flatter than a plate full of piss and the item system adds needless complexity.  But other than that it's fine.

Local multiplayer is near perfect.  Almost everything you would expect is there but nothing that detracts from it's identity.  I'd like to have seen some handicap options as my only local opponent is my 9 year old daughter.  It's like if it were Goku vs. Krillin in dbs.  I can't really go all out on her.  It would be cool to give her the win if she could land a single combo string on me or something rather than me having the drop the quality of my already poor quality play to give her the W or make it close.

Online play.  Shew... There is a ranked and casual match making system.  You can edit the options before hand to try and find only folks that have a good connection to you.  Seems to work well because I've not had any lag during any of my matches.  So at least for me, online felt about as good as local.  But now I am going to talk a bit more about how exactly games seem to play out.  Every single character can execute nice looking combo strings by repeatedly pressing a single button.  Some characters will even mix in lows and overheads.  Veterans who have spent a lot of time with the game will know what is coming and when.  Noobies like myself who has not memorized every characters combo strings are at a disadvantage.  But needless to say knowing how to block and counter with some sort of punish is important.  And I mentioned earlier that I may be noob when it comes to thinking some of the elaborate combo's aren't viable in actual matches.  But hot damn. Most of the folks I have played against were exceptionally deadly if they landed even one attack.  I've been combo'd for nearly half a characters health multiple times by very grand and impressive looking combo's.  I have managed to squeak out the occasional win against these behemoths with shear fundamentals.  It really felt like I had to outplay my opponent constantly because one slip up from me was devastating.  I'm going to say it's great because I did enjoy the challenge and I felt next to no lag.  But if you are not willing to invest the time you will get smoked.  I never once played against a person similar to my skill level or lower.  To be expected as old as the game is - everyone active online seems to have the ability to be somewhat competitive.  Side note: Not a dead game as of this review.  Always tons of folks in the lobby ready to que up.  Never had to wait long for a match.

Lastly... DLC content.  I'm not new to the concept.  But this def pops my cherry for how monetization works in modern fighting games.  I bought the game on sale with a fighting pass that came with a few of the oldest DLC characters.  I still lack 12 characters.  Even if they go on sale at half price for 2.50$USD I'm still looking at 30$ to complete the collection.  On top of the (I think it was 15$ paid for the deal at the time) for the base game and a few extras.  Which is a bit steep imo for how old the game is.  But not terrible since you can acquire everything for roughly 50$USD if it's on sale.  And you are encouraged to buy the DLC character's.  They all seem better than the original in the base game via various means.  More overheads and lows in there combo's to force your opponent to be more proactive with blocking.  Downright quicker, maybe more range on a few attacks.  It's all there.  You can win with base game characters,  But your work is cut out for you.  I complain about cost because the age of the game.  But if you are really having a good time it's not that bad of value - again, with a sale.  Also kind of sucks how some characters are simply outclassed and become jokes.  I guess that is also just like the show too though.

Oh and there is also an in game currency you earn perpetually that is used to unlock color schemes for characters and various things for your lobby avatar.  Unlocks work in a loot box type manner and you can earn duplicates but those seem to turn into a special currency.  But when you use that special currency, to my understanding, you cannot get duplicates.  A round about way to have you play more.  Also if you are playing in an online lobby around certain holidays there are certain things that can only be unlocked during those holidays.  So that is kind of neat.

Overall to super summarize I do recommend.  Even to newer folks to the genre.  Especially to fans of dragonball.  If you are a fan of both what have you been doing with your life to not have this?  All the characters have iconic attacks from the franchise.  It feels good, looks good and sounds good.  Expect no quarter this far in to the games life cycle when it comes to online play.  Everyone is dangerous and absolute monsters.  Prepare for a challenge.  However, I would only recommend buying on sale.  The full price for the base game and all DLC combined is absurd.  But an easier pill to swallow when at least 50% off.

It’s 2026 now, and I can say this confidently: despite dropping the game at a competitive level in 2021—and despite fully walking away from it multiple times for months at a stretch since then—this is a good game. At this point, we can accept that.

Is it very different from anything else on the market?
Yes.

Does that make it a fake fighting game?
No. It just makes it unique.

Do you have to learn Dragon Ball instead of playing it like a traditional fighting game?
Also yes. But I don’t play Guilty Gear the way I play Melty Blood, and I don’t play KOF the way I play either of those—so that feels pretty normal, honestly.

If you’ve never played a fighting game before and want something approachable—easy starter combos, straightforward game plans, relatively generalized frame data, and no immediate need to learn deep character-specific knowledge—this game is a great place to start and have fun. I write this as someone who generally doesn't enjoy fighting games; FighterZ is the one and only traditional fighting game that has ever managed to hook me, with well over 800 hours across all the platforms I've played it on. The reason for that is simple, it's one of the few fighting games I've played that is easy to both understand and pick up and play. My biggest issue with other games of this genre is that while their systems have great depth, to reach that depth you have to cross multiple barriers before you can begin having fun, and one of them is the input combinations. I simply don't care for the obsession of other games for making me do God of War quick time events for even the most basic moves, it ruins the fun for me. Not the case here, everything from specials to supers is simple and straightforward; a Quarter-Circle + a Button, that's it. There's no BS, to hoops to jump through, just an open invitation to learn the systems at play. This makes a world of difference in being able to enjoy the game, it allows you to focus on learning the neutral, playing mind-games, bettering your defense, learning advanced combos, practicing team-synergy, creating set-ups and mix-ups, all without having to worry about whether or not my hand will be able to pull off the move I want to use. For this, it's one of few competitive games where I've been able to have fun right off the bat, while improving my skills constantly too.

This is all without mentioning how gorgeous the presentation of the game is, doing true justice to the show's artsyle, looking 2D while being 3D with many techniques like frame timing, model manipulation, smears, impact frames, and more 
coming together to make it feel true to the anime. It's clear the devs love the series and wanted to do it justice, as every move from every fighter is a direct reference to either the manga, anime, or a previous game, all the while not compromising game-feel. And of course, the Dramatic Finishes that re-create some of the most iconic moments of the series are some of the coolest things I've ever witnessed. The game does such a fantastic job at being like the show, that at times, for as tacky as it is to say nowadays, it really did make me feel like I was in an actual Dragon Ball battle.

Words alone can't do it justice to how much I love this game. As a Dragon Ball fan, it's a love letter to the series, and as a videogame, it's the fighting game I've dreamed of my whole life. One of my all-time favorite video-games.

This game is an absolute blast to play casually.  You can pick it up and immediately pull off amazing looking combos and shoot Ki blasts while flying through the air.  For me, this is the closest a game has come to feeling like you're actually playing an episode of DBZ or Super.  Movements are fluid, combos are crisp, animations are perfect, and hits are impactful.  The story mode is lackluster, but passable enough as an excuse to learn the basics.

Once you get past using Autocombos and start learning the actual fighting system underneath, there is no end to the depths of the combos you can pull off.  It feels like an even faster BlazBlue, with combo strings of 20+ inputs.  You will find yourself pulling off a normal combo, launching your opponent into the air, comboing them into a wall bounce, grabbing in the air into a sliding knockdown, and calling an assist to keep the opponent juggled while you reset and start the combo again.  Input buffering makes it fairly simple to pull these combos off, though it becomes trickier online if you have a large frame delay.

Note that I said simple, not easy.  This is a game you can play casually and never touch the depths of the systems, or a game you can lose hundreds of hours in if you choose to master its mechanics fully.  It's rare to find a game that handles both well, but DBFZ manages to do so.

At this point, there is not a huge community, but I really don't have trouble finding online matches when I want them.  It's old enough now though that I would definitely wait for a sale -- it's 90% off during most sales.  If you have any interest in DB or Fighting games, as you probably do if you're reading this, it's absolutely worth picking up for $6.
